title: Trauma: the event, timing and reliving
about: Questions on whether a frightening event is part of the picture, how long ago it happened (reactions in the first month are expected and often settle), and the reliving, avoidance and on-guard features that follow it. Ask at the client's pace; detail is not needed in a first conversation.

questions.text: Has something happened to the client, or in front of them, that was terrifying or dangerous, such as an assault, a serious accident, combat, abuse or a disaster?
questions.why: Trauma-related patterns start from a frightening event; without one, the same symptoms point elsewhere. Ask gently, let the client choose how much to share, and do not press for detail early on.

options.label: The client prefers not to say right now
options.note: Respect the choice; offer grounding skills and come back to it when the client is ready.

questions.text: When did the event happen, and how long have the reactions lasted?
questions.why: Strong reactions in the first month after an event are common and often settle with support (an acute stress reaction). A trauma pattern such as PTSD is considered when they last beyond about a month; reactions can also begin months later.

options.label: Under 2 weeks
options.note: Early reactions often settle. Offer practical support, psychoeducation and grounding, check safety, and plan a check-in within the month.

options.label: 2 to 4 weeks
options.note: Still within the first month: watch the course, check safety and support, and consider brief trauma-focused CBT if reactions are marked or not easing. Reassess at about one month.

questions.text: Does the client relive the event through unwanted memories, nightmares or flashbacks?
questions.why: Reliving the event, rather than simply remembering it, is a key feature of a trauma reaction and helps choose between trauma-focused approaches.

options.label: Flashbacks: it feels as if it is happening again

questions.text: Does the client keep away from thoughts, conversations, places or people that bring the event back?
questions.why: Avoiding reminders keeps the memory from being processed and is a key target of trauma-focused treatment.

questions.text: Since the event, is the client constantly on guard, or easily and strongly startled?
questions.why: A body that stays on alert after the danger has passed is common after trauma and often drives poor sleep, irritability and poor concentration.

options.label: Constantly on guard, scanning for danger
